sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to the M/M/c Task Queuing Dynamics Studio. Incoming tasks arrive on the left and dispatch across c parallel worker stations on the right. With 10 workers at 2.5 tasks per minute handling 18 tasks per minute, utilization is 72 percent and delay is low. Push arrivals past 25 to watch the queue explode asymptotically.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the queue visualization canvas, Dr. Nova! Ingesting 26 tasks per minute with a 25 task capacity pushes utilization over 100 percent, turning the buffer bright red!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1: A labeling queue runs with 10 annotators each completing 3 tasks per minute. At 28.5 tasks per minute, utilization is 95 percent. A scraper surge increases arrivals by just 6 percent to 30.2 tasks per minute. What happens mathematically to the queue?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Kaito, let's see if our engineers can spot what happens to Erlang-C delays when a 95 percent loaded queue experiences a 6 percent arrival surge!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Spot on, System Architect! Total workforce capacity is 10 times 3.0, or 30 tasks per minute. At 30.2 arrivals, utilization rho exceeds 1.0. By M/M/c queuing theory, steady-state Erlang-C collapses and wait time diverges to infinity, accumulating 0.2 unserviceable tasks every minute.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Not quite. Remember that when arrival rate lambda exceeds total capacity c times mu, utilization crosses 1.0. In queuing theory, steady-state Erlang-C distributions collapse and wait times diverge to infinity rather than increasing linearly.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: In the Wald SPRT Worker Quality Studio, watch the cumulative log-likelihood ratio trajectory. Submitting accurate honeypot labels steps downward toward the green certification boundary at minus 2.25. Submitting erroneous labels steps upward toward the red suspension boundary at plus 2.89.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the SPRT chart, Dr. Nova! Two quick honeypot errors shoot the trajectory straight past plus 2.89, triggering instant fraud suspension!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2: An object detector assists video annotators. Scratch annotation takes 30 seconds, verifying an accurate box takes 4 seconds, and repairing a flawed box takes 42 seconds. At 25 percent model accuracy, what is the throughput multiplier and break-even accuracy?

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Manual annotation takes 30 seconds, verification takes 4, and correction takes 42! At 25 percent proposal accuracy, does the team speed up or slow down?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Precisely right! The break-even accuracy is 42 minus 30 divided by 42 minus 4, which equals 31.6 percent. At 25 percent accuracy, the effective speedup is 0.923x. Annotators suffer negative speedup, working 8.3 percent slower than starting from scratch!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Not quite. Because repairing flawed proposals takes 42 seconds compared to 30 seconds from scratch, bad proposals actively slow down annotators. The break-even threshold is 31.6 percent, so 25 percent accuracy yields 0.923x negative speedup.
